newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PNG rebels say they would consider reopening mine.
newsitem.headline: PNG rebels say they would consider reopening mine.

text.p: Secessionist rebels on Papua New Guinea's Bougainville island would consider allowing a vast copper mine to reopen after talks were held on independence for the island, an Australian newspaper reported on Saturday.

Bougainville Revolutionary Army (BRA) commander Sam Kauona said the BRA would only discuss reopening the Panguna mine if future talks with Papua New Guinea included independence for the island, 800 km (500 miles) northeast of the capital Port Moresby.

The rebels were "ready to entertain any other issues, for instance mining or economic matters" after those negotiations, The Age quoted Kauona as saying in an interview at a mountain base on the resource-rich island.

The Panguna copper-gold mine, owned by Anglo-Australian mining giant RTZ-CRA, has been idle since rebel attacks on workers forced its closure in May 1989. It provided a third of Papua New Guinea's foreign exchange at the time.

Kauona, who said an unofficial ceasefire was in place on the island, also called on Australia to back a plan to bring United Nations peacekeeping troops to the island while independence talks are held.
Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan stepped aside in March after it was revealed he had hired mercenaries to help put down the rebellion and reopen the mine.

An inquiry is being held into the failed US$36 million mercenary plan, which sparked the South Pacific nation's worst crisis since independence from Australia was granted in 1975. An election is due to be held next month.
"There seems to be no threat from Papua New Guinea at this time," Kauona said.
"You can assume there is an unofficial ceasefire."
Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer however said a peace settlement would have to be reached before U.N. troops could become involved.
"The international community isn't going to send peacekeepers into a sovereign country uninvited to keep a peace that hasn't even been negotiated," The Age quoted Downer as saying.

Gerard Sinato, premier of the Papua New Guinea-appointed Bougainville Transitional Government, called for a meeting to be held in Australia between the rebels and Bougainvilleans loyal to Port Moresby.
"I would like to see Bougainville leaders talk outside Bougainville," Sinato said.
